paras: The killing of Berry's brother at Tippecanoe, Ohio, was the fatal shooting of an unnamed Black man by the marshal of New Philadelphia in mid-August 1895, during an attempt to arrest his brother, a "colored man" named Berry. The marshal was wounded in the wrist and Berry escaped, and the episode reached readers outside Ohio only as a brief wire item.

According to a dispatch from Cadiz dated August 16, Berry was wanted in Tuscarawas county "to stand trial for an assault," and the marshal of New Philadelphia went to Tippecanoe to take him back. Neither Berry's brother nor the marshal is named in the report.

When the marshal tried to make the arrest, the dispatch said, Berry and his brother, "who had a revolver, resisted arrest, and shooting commenced." The marshal was shot through the wrist but fired three bullets into the brother's breast, killing him instantly. Berry got away carrying a shotgun, and the report claimed he "would have killed the marshal, in all probability, but his gun missed fire." The account does not say who fired first, and it rests entirely on the officer's side of the encounter.
No report of an inquest, of Berry's recapture, or of any inquiry into the marshal's conduct appears in the coverage.

The episode survives in a single wire dispatch, run under the headline "Killed by a Town Marshal" by the Wilmington Daily Republican in Delaware and the Evening Herald of Shenandoah, Pennsylvania, both on August 16, 1895. The two papers printed the text word for word, presenting the marshal's account of armed resistance as fact and describing him as having "succeeded in planting three bullets in the brother's breast." Berry was identified by race and the killed man only by his relation to Berry, and no Black-press coverage of the shooting was found.
